title: A log-scale bar chart of cost is read as ratios, so the right question is how many times slower, not how many seconds
summary: The top row shows two sampled curves per method; the bottom bars compare the measured wall-clock time to draw 100 samples on a logarithmic axis. Equal distances on that axis are equal ratios, and the printed times give a slowest-to-fastest ratio of about 11,000, about four decades.

media.alt: Top row: four small line plots, titled Class A to Class D with their method names, each showing two smooth increasing kappa(T) curves against temperature from 300 to 2500 kelvin. Bottom: four horizontal bars on a logarithmic time axis from 0.01 to 1000 seconds. Class B is longest at 204.3 seconds per 100 samples, Class D 5.52 seconds, Class C 0.02 seconds, Class A 0.018 seconds.

source.caption: Measured sampling cost across all four classes -- five orders of magnitude
source.note: Group explainer. The live poster is the last frame of a video in which each panel's timer runs at its measured rate; its numbers (7.2 ms, 81.72 s, 8.0 ms, 2.21 s for 40 samples) agree with the bar chart when scaled from 100 samples.
group: 13_four_classes_static: Measured sampling cost across all four classes (representative)
12_four_classes_live_poster: All four sampling-method classes, live, one frame: 40 samples each, with a compute-time readout per panel

read_the_figure.question: How much does each sampling method cost, and do the sampled curves look comparable enough for the cost difference to matter?
read_the_figure.axes: Top row: x is temperature T in kelvin (300 to 2500); y is kappa(T) = k_sample / k_nominal, a dimensionless ratio; each panel has its own y range. Bottom bars: x is the measured wall-clock time to generate 100 samples, in seconds, on a log scale from 0.01 to 1000; each bar is labelled with the time and the time per sample in milliseconds.
look_at: The bar lengths are logarithms of time: the distance between two bars is the ratio of their times. The slowest bar (B, 204.3 s) and the fastest (A, 0.018 s) are about four decades apart on the axis, not three and not five.
Read the printed per-sample times: A 0.18 ms, C 0.2 ms, D 55.2 ms, B about 2,040 ms. A and C are the same within rounding; D is about 276 times C; B is about 37 times D.

Top row: all four classes produce smooth, monotone curves of similar scale (kappa from about 20 to 35 for B, C and D). Class A's panel starts near 0 at low temperature and rises to about 27, and its panel label names a different reaction from the other three.
The bars are not sorted: the order is D, C, B, A from top to bottom.
read_the_figure.proves: That the four methods produce curves with a similar look at wildly different cost. It supports a cost comparison; it does not on its own support a claim of equivalent output quality.
if_wrong: A cost axis that starts at zero on a linear scale would hide A and C completely (they would be invisible next to B): that is why a log axis is the right form here.
Panels labelled with different reactions invite a false comparison of the curves.
A time per sample computed from one run, with no repeat, may be affected by machine load.
must_check: Time is measured on the same machine for the same number of samples in every bar.
Several repetitions or an error bar are shown: not on this figure.
The same reaction is used in all panels being compared.
A log axis is labelled as such and its decades are counted before claiming 'orders of magnitude'.
Bars are sorted or the order is explained.
as_drawn: Printed times per 100 samples: A 0.018 s, B 204.3 s, C 0.02 s, D 5.52 s.

Ratio of the slowest to the fastest, computed: 204.3 / 0.018 = 11,350, which is 4.05 decades. The figure title says 'five orders of magnitude'; the log axis spans five decades, but the data span about four.
Live poster (40 samples): A 7.2 ms, B 81.72 s, C 8.0 ms, D 2.21 s. Scaling the bar chart's per-sample times by 40 gives 7.2 ms, 81.7 s, 8.0 ms and 2.2 s: consistent.
The Class A panel is labelled n-C7H16 + HO2 -> C7H15-2 + H2O2 while the other three are labelled n-C7H16 + H -> C7H15-3 + H2, although the figure title says same reaction family.

terms.meaning: Elapsed real time for a task, as opposed to processor time. It includes waiting and depends on the machine.
A factor of ten. 'k orders of magnitude' means a ratio of ten to the k.
An axis on which equal distances represent equal ratios. A bar's length is then proportional to the logarithm of the value, not the value.
A method that finishes in a fixed, small number of operations. Classes A and C are described this way on the figure.
A method that improves a guess repeatedly until a tolerance is met. Its cost grows with the number of parameters and iterations. Classes B and D use it.
Total time divided by the number of samples. It is what matters when the number of samples is chosen freely.
The ratio of the slower time to the faster time.

remember: On a log axis the distance between two bars is a ratio: 4 decades is a factor of 10,000.
Count decades from the data, not from the axis limits.
Total cost is the number of samples times the cost per sample, so cost scales linearly with sample count for independent draws.
Equal-looking output is a claim that needs its own evidence, such as a comparison of the sampled distributions.
A single timing is a sample of a noisy quantity: repeat it.

understand.title: Why closed-form and iterative methods differ in cost
understand.text: A closed-form solve answers in one linear-algebra step, a fraction of a millisecond. An iterative optimiser has to evaluate the problem many times before it stops, so every sample costs seconds. The figure shows this as a gap of about four decades.

understand.title: Why the top row matters
understand.text: A cost comparison is only meaningful if the products are comparable. The top row shows that all four produce curves of a similar kind; that is the reason to compare costs at all. It does not prove their distributions agree, and the Class A panel is labelled with a different reaction.

understand.title: Why a log axis
understand.text: Times from 0.018 to 204 seconds cannot share a linear axis: the two fast bars would vanish. On the log axis every bar is visible and equal steps mean equal ratios. The price is that bar length no longer means time: read the numbers.

steps.title: Ratio from printed times
steps.note: Divide the two printed times for 100 samples. The number of samples cancels because it is the same for both.

steps.title: Count the decades
steps.note: A ratio of about 11,350 is just over four orders of magnitude. The bar chart's axis spans five decades (0.01 to 1000), which is where 'five' can come from.

steps.title: Cost per sample
steps.note: The printed per-sample times are the totals divided by 100, which checks the labels: 204.3 s over 100 is 2.043 s, i.e. 2.04e3 ms.

steps.title: Cost scales linearly with samples
steps.note: For independent draws the total grows in proportion to N. The live poster stops at 40 samples; 40 times each per-sample cost reproduces its timers (7.2 ms, 81.7 s, 8.0 ms, 2.2 s).

steps.title: Bar length on a log axis
steps.note: Bars start at the left edge of the axis (0.01 s here), so they show how far each value is above the axis minimum in decades, not its size.

steps.title: Decision: samples needed
steps.note: The practical use of the figure: with a fixed time budget the number of affordable samples is the budget over the per-sample cost, and it differs by the same factor as the costs.

worked.title: How long would 10,000 samples take?
worked.problem: Using the printed per-sample costs, estimate the time to draw 10,000 samples for Class B (2.043 s each) and Class A (0.18 ms each).
worked.answer: About 5.7 hours against about 1.8 seconds, assuming the per-sample cost stays constant and independent of the machine load.

analyze.q: Class A and Class C differ by only 11 percent in the printed total (0.018 against 0.02). What would you need to know before ranking them?
The title says five orders of magnitude and the data give four. Which is a fair statement, and what is the error a reader might make from the axis?
analyze.hint: Decades of axis versus decades of data.

analyze.q: Class D uses an iterative solver on a reduced problem and costs 276 times Class C's time. What does that suggest about the cost of iteration relative to a closed-form solve?

evaluate.q: Is the claim 'statistically equivalent output' (made on the page) supported by this figure? What evidence would support it?
evaluate.hint: Compare distributions of the samples, not their appearance.

evaluate.q: Redesign the bar chart so that it cannot be misread. List three changes.
evaluate.hint: Sort bars, mark decades, show repeats, label the axis as log.

create: Add to the figure a second axis that gives time as a multiple of the fastest method.
Design a benchmark that repeats each measurement and reports the median and range.

checks.q: Why use a logarithmic axis for this chart?
checks.hint: What happens to the two fast bars on a linear axis?
checks.answer: The times span four decades. On a linear axis the two fast bars would be invisible next to the slowest; on a log axis all bars are readable and equal distances mean equal ratios.

checks.q: Method X takes 0.5 s per 100 samples and method Y takes 50 s. By how many orders of magnitude do they differ?
checks.answer: The ratio is 100, so two orders of magnitude.

checks.q: Using only the figure's printed numbers, what is the ratio of Class B's time to Class D's?
checks.answer: About 37, which is a bit over one and a half decades.

checks.q: Does a four-decade cost difference prove the cheap method is the better one?
checks.answer: No. Cost is only one criterion; you also need evidence that the samples are equally valid for the purpose, and you need the cost of anything else in the pipeline.

checks.q: What extra panel would make this figure support the claim of equivalent output?
checks.hint: A direct comparison of sample statistics.
checks.answer: A panel comparing the sample distributions of the four classes (for example the mean and spread of kappa at a few temperatures, or an overlay of their envelopes) computed on the same reaction.
